The six-hour handover, and the average that hides it

Northwick Analytics · fictional case note · invented throughout

Every depot we have looked at reports a handover average, and every one of those averages is technically correct and practically useless. A depot averaging ninety minutes is almost never a depot where handovers take ninety minutes.

It is a depot where most take forty, and four a week take six hours. Those four are the entire operational problem, and the average is the one number that structurally cannot show them to you.

Where the time actually goes

A handover has three timestamps that already exist on the handheld: the seal scan when the driver arrives, the weighbridge slip, and the supervisor sign-off that releases the trailer.

Nobody set out to build a measurement system. Those three exist for completely different reasons, and the gaps between them were never meant to be read as anything.

But the gaps are where the trailer sits still. That is the whole insight, and it is not sophisticated.

The first gap

Seal scan to weighbridge. This one is usually short and usually honest. A trailer arrives, it gets weighed, the slip prints.

When it is long, the cause is almost always physical: the weighbridge is occupied, or it is out of calibration and somebody has driven to the next yard.

The second gap

Weighbridge to sign-off. This is where the six hours live.

The trailer is weighed, the paperwork does not match, and the discrepancy goes into a process that nobody has ever drawn on a wall. A supervisor rings a planner. The planner rings the customer. The customer is at lunch.

Meanwhile the trailer occupies a bay, the driver runs down their hours, and none of that appears anywhere as a cost attributable to a paperwork mismatch.

The yard does not have a waiting problem. It has a decision-making problem that expresses itself as waiting.

Why the average survives anyway

Three reasons, all of them reasonable from inside the business.

  • It is the number that was asked for, years ago, by somebody who has since left.
  • It is comparable across depots, and comparability feels like rigour.
  • It moves slowly, which makes it a comfortable thing to put in a monthly pack.
  • Nobody has ever been asked to defend it, because nobody has ever disputed it.

None of those are stupid. They are what happens when a measure outlives the question it was built to answer.

What replacing it costs

Less than people expect, because the replacement is not a new metric. It is a list.

The list has one row per handover that is still open, with the depot, the shift, and how long it has been sitting. It is not an average of anything.

  • No new fields for drivers.
  • No new hardware in the yard.
  • No change to how a supervisor works, beyond opening one page at the start of a shift.

What we got wrong first

The first version of this ranked depots against each other. It was accurate, it was well received in the room, and it was quietly ignored for six weeks.

The reason was obvious in hindsight. A league table tells a supervisor something about their depot's standing and nothing at all about what to do before lunch.

The second version dropped ranking entirely and listed only open handovers. It was used the first morning it existed.

The thing that nearly killed it

An early build sent an email at six in the morning summarising the previous day. It was requested, it was built, and it was the single most disliked thing we shipped.

Supervisors read it on their phones before they were on site, could do nothing about any of it, and arrived already behind. We removed it and did not replace it.

Where this does not apply

A yard with genuinely uniform handovers gets nothing from this. If the distribution really is tight around the mean, the mean is a fine summary and the list will be empty most days.

We have not yet seen one, but we have only looked at eleven depots, and all eleven came to us because somebody already suspected they had a problem.

That is a biased sample and it should be read as one.

This article is invented in full. Northwick Analytics, the depots, the figures and the quotations do not exist. It is committed as a parser fixture and nothing in it should be read as a claim about any real organisation.
